extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and psychology; readers interested in the scientific status and methodology of the study of human nature
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for treating human thoughts, feelings, and actions as the subject of scientific inquiry (i.e., what makes the study of mind a science, what laws of mind are, and how they are to be discovered).

rubrics_metrics.name: Science requires constant laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Any facts are fitted to be a subject of science which follow one another according to constant laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A phenomenon can be scientific even if the laws are not yet discovered or are not practically predictable with present resources (example: meteorological phenomena). The essential requirement is that phenomena depend on laws (uniformities of succession) even if our observations are imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness depends on comprehending all causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A science becomes exact when its laws 'comprehend the whole of the causes by which the phenomena are influenced' and assign to each cause the share of effect which really belongs to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by astronomy (exact once perturbations were accounted for) versus tidology/meteorology (inexact because minor or local causes are not fully ascertained). Exactness is not an intrinsic impossibility but depends on ability to ascertain minor causes and their effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate generalizations can constitute scientific knowledge when they account for the principal causes and when their limits are understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For social/political purposes, approximate generalizations are often sufficient; however, to be genuinely scientific they should be connected deductively with the laws of nature from which they result so the proper limits and anticipations for new circumstances can be deduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of laws of mind vs laws of body
rubrics_metrics.description: A law of Mind is when a state of mind is produced by another state of mind; a law of Body is when a state of mind is produced directly by a state of body (physiology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensation immediate antecedents are bodily states and belong to physiology; other mental states may have bodily antecedents but their successions must be studied in mental phenomena themselves because we lack direct knowledge of the corresponding nervous states.

rubrics_metrics.name: All mental states have immediate causes
rubrics_metrics.description: All states of mind are immediately caused either by other states of mind, or by states of body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if physiological antecedents exist, we currently know the succession of mental states only by observing mental phenomena; thus psychological laws are legitimate objects of study rather than being reducible entirely to known physiological laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychology requires direct observation and experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The successions which obtain among mental phenomena must be ascertained by observation and experiment of those phenomena themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we are ignorant of the characteristics of the supposed nervous antecedents, mental science should not be subsumed under physiology solely on the grounds that mental states have bodily antecedents. Psychological analysis remains indispensable.

rubrics_metrics.name: First general law of mind (impression -> idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever any state of consciousness has once been excited in us, an inferior degree of the same state (an idea) is capable of being reproduced without the original external cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed in Hume's language: 'every mental impression has its idea.' Examples: remembering sights, feelings, or imagined objects without re‑presentation of the external cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of Association (three principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas or secondary mental states are excited by impressions or by other ideas according to laws of association: (1) similar ideas tend to excite one another; (2) when two impressions have been frequently experienced together or in immediate succession, recurrence of one tends to excite the other (contiguity/conjunction); (3) greater intensity in impressions is equivalent to greater frequency in rendering them excitable by one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as principal and experimentally ascertained laws of association; reference given to James Mill's Analysis for many applications and exemplifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental chemistry / generation of complex ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex mental phenomena may be generated from simpler impressions or ideas in a manner analogous to chemical combination: simple ideas may 'melt and coalesce' into a complex idea that appears simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When elements coalesce so their separate elements are not consciously distinguishable, it is proper to say complex ideas are generated by simpler ones rather than merely composed of them. Examples: blended sensations producing a unified perception; notion of orange consisting of several sensory elements yet felt as one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal proof requires Method of Difference beyond Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that one phenomenon (e.g., Belief) is caused by another (e.g., close association of ideas), evidence of mere concurrence (Method of Agreement) is insufficient; the more conclusive Method of Difference is required to establish causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even strong regular association, without tests that remove or alter the purported cause, cannot conclusively prove causal generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology cautions: avoid misleading term 'Necessity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the term 'Necessity' for the simple fact of causation is misleading because in common use 'necessity' implies irresistibleness; for causation it is better to speak of uniformity of order and predictability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misuse of 'necessity' fosters fatalistic feelings; distinguishing 'necessity' (irresistibleness) from causal predictability prevents confusion and the erroneous practical consequences of language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character formation and moral freedom criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is formed both by circumstances and 'by' the agent: one can, by willing the requisite means, make oneself different; moral freedom is the consciousness that habits or temptations are not one's masters but can be resisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The wish to alter character is itself shaped by experience; a confirmed character (purpose independent of pleasure) constitutes fuller moral freedom; practical consequences differ between thinking change impossible and having no desire to change.
